name: Google homepage (original)
lesson: A view earns one focal point: when everything else is deleted, the eye cannot miss the action you want taken.
why: While AltaVista and Yahoo crammed 100+ links, banners, and directories above the fold, Google shipped roughly 30 words on a white page: a wordmark, one centered text input, and two buttons. It passes the squint test at any blur radius — the input field is the only landable surface on the screen.
fal_prompt: Recreate the circa-1998-2000 Google homepage in pure HTML/CSS: full white viewport; vertically centered stack containing a multicolor serif-style wordmark (blue/red/yellow/green letterforms approximated with styled spans), below it a single 1px-inset bordered text input about 320px wide, and two small gray Windows-95-style beveled buttons ('Google Search', 'I'm Feeling Lucky') with 2px outset borders; 10px Arial footer links in #0000CC at the bottom; everything centered, enormous empty margins on all sides. The recreation must make the emptiness itself legible as the design decision.

name: Craigslist homepage
lesson: Hierarchy can be built from nothing but grouping, order, and weight — no images, no color system, no chrome.
why: Roughly 200 plain underlined links on white, organized into labeled category columns (community, housing, jobs, for sale...), in essentially one typeface and three colors: #0000EE link blue, visited purple, black bold column headers. The page has survived 25+ years nearly unchanged because column grouping and reading order alone carry the entire information hierarchy.
fal_prompt: Recreate the classic Craigslist homepage grid in HTML/CSS: white background, a narrow left rail with a small bordered search box and stacked utility links, then five tight columns of category lists; each column starts with a bold black lowercase header ('community', 'housing', 'jobs', 'for sale', 'services') followed by 10-15 underlined #0000EE links in ~13px Times/Arial with minimal line spacing; a few visited-purple links mixed in; no images, no icons, no shadows, no rounded corners. Spacing between columns ~20px. The point is to show hierarchy emerging purely from grouping and bold headers.
verify_note: Started as an email list in 1995; the website went live in 1996, so the year is correct for the homepage.

name: GOV.UK redesign
designer: Government Digital Service (design lead Ben Terrett); New Transport type by Margaret Calvert & Henrik Kubel
lesson: When the typeface, sizes, and black-on-white contrast are right, type alone can be the entire interface.
why: One typeface — New Transport, a screen adaptation of the 1960s UK road-sign alphabet commissioned in Light and Bold — set black on white under a solid black masthead, with large left-aligned headings and almost zero decoration. This near-typographic-only website beat the Shard and the Olympic cauldron to win Design Museum Design of the Year 2013.
fal_prompt: Recreate a 2012-13 GOV.UK service page in HTML/CSS: solid black masthead bar (~50px) with a white crown-placeholder mark and 'GOV.UK' set in a humanist sans (Transport-like; use a geometric-humanist fallback stack); below, on white, a 1.5-line 48px bold black page heading, a 19px lede paragraph, 19px body text in a ~640px measure, blue #005EA5 underlined links, and a left-aligned green #00823B 'Start now' button with a right-pointing arrow; thin #BFC1C3 horizontal rules between sections. No images, no gradients, no shadows — typography and a single black bar do all the work.
verify_note: Verified: launched Oct 2012, won Design Museum Design of the Year 2013; New Transport screen weights by Calvert & Kubel confirmed.

name: iA.net — "Web Design Is 95% Typography"
lesson: Setting body text — size, measure, leading — is the core engineering act of web design, not the garnish.
why: Reichenstein's October 2006 essay and iA's own site argued for treating the web as typography: at a time when 11-12px body text was standard, iA demanded a 16px-minimum '100%, Easy-to-Read' body size and demonstrated it with a single chrome-free column of generously leaded text. The essay reframed web design as macro-typography and directly preceded the large-type reading web (Medium, Readability, Safari Reader).
fal_prompt: Recreate the 2006 iA.net article view in HTML/CSS: pale off-white background, one centered text column ~30em wide, body text at a then-radical 16-18px Georgia/serif with 1.5+ line-height, a large plain headline, modest gray metadata line, no sidebar, no images, no navigation chrome beyond a small wordmark top-left; paragraphs separated by a full blank line. Include a side-by-side comparison strip showing the same paragraph set at 11px Verdana (the 2006 norm) versus 16px Georgia to make the essay's argument visible.

name: Medium reading view
designer: Medium design team (Ev Williams; 2013 type system in FF Tisa & Freight Sans)
lesson: Whitespace is the material — ma: one measured column where the empty margin, not decoration, creates the reading room.
why: A single ~700px column of FF Tisa serif at roughly 21px with ~1.58 line-height, giving 65-75 characters per line, floating in a viewport where the margins occupy more area than the text; no sidebar, no related-links rail, no ads. The proportions — not any visual styling — are what made 'reads like Medium' a compliment the whole industry chased.

Annotate nothing — the recreation must demonstrate that margin area visibly exceeds text area.
verify_note: Medium launched 2012 with FF Meta Serif/Myriad and switched to FF Tisa + Freight Sans in 2013 — the item's framing of a 2013 type system is accurate.

name: Stripe API Reference (two-pane docs)
designer: Stripe design & engineering team (Patrick & John Collison's company)
lesson: A grid can encode the structure of the content itself — prose and code as two locked, scroll-synced columns.
why: Stripe's API reference split every endpoint into a white prose column on the left and a dark code-example pane on the right, scroll-synchronized so explanation and example never separate. The layout was so canonical that Slate (2013) was built explicitly 'inspired by Stripe's API docs' and the two-pane pattern became the default grammar of API documentation industry-wide.

The two main columns must read as one synced grid row per endpoint.
verify_note: Stripe launched publicly Sept 2011; its multi-column API reference is widely credited as the canonical pattern and Slate (2013) explicitly cites it as inspiration.

name: FT.com 'Next FT' redesign
designer: Financial Times design team (Origami design system); Financier typeface by Kris Sowersby, Klim Type Foundry
lesson: Material honesty on the web: carry your physical heritage — the FT's pink newsprint — into the pixel as a true background color.
why: The Next FT rollout set the entire site on 'paper' #FFF1E5, a digital translation of the salmon newsprint the FT has printed on since 1893, with near-black ink text, a restrained teal accent (#0D7680), and headlines in Financier — a serif Kris Sowersby drew for the FT's 2014 redesign. One inherited background color does the brand work that competitors attempt with logos and banners.

No pure white anywhere — every surface must sit on the salmon paper tone.

name: Bloomberg Terminal
lesson: Color as encoded meaning, never decoration: a fixed semantic palette that users read preattentively for forty years.
why: Black ground with amber/orange field labels, green and red strictly reserved for up/down and go/stop, and a custom keyboard whose colored keys (green GO, red CANCEL, yellow market-sector keys) mirror the on-screen code. The palette has stayed essentially frozen since the 1980s because traders parse it faster than text — proof that a stable color code beats a fashionable one.
fal_prompt: Documentary photograph of a financial trading desk at night in a dark office: a dual-screen professional market terminal glowing with dense amber-orange and green character grids on black, screens slightly out of focus so no characters are legible; in the sharp foreground a distinctive professional keyboard with clusters of yellow, green, and red keys; reflections of the amber glow on a coffee mug and the desk surface; shallow depth of field, 35mm lens look, moody low ambient light with the screens as the only light source, cinematic realism, no readable text, no logos, no watermarks.
verify_note: Market Master terminal shipped December 1982; co-founders also included Duncan MacMillan and Charles Zegar, but the named pair is accurate.

name: Solarized color palette
lesson: Build palettes on measured lightness relationships in a perceptual color space, not on hues picked by eye.
why: Exactly sixteen colors — eight monotones plus eight accents — designed in CIELAB so the monotones have symmetric lightness steps: flipping between dark mode (base #002B36) and light mode (base #FDF6E3) preserves identical perceived contrast, and the accents sit at fixed color-wheel relationships. Published March 2011, it became the most-ported color scheme in software because the math, not taste, guarantees it works everywhere.
fal_prompt: Hand-code an SVG diagram of the Solarized system: two horizontal rows of eight rounded-rect swatches — top row the monotones from #002B36 through #FDF6E3 arranged along a labeled CIELAB lightness axis (L* values 15 to 97 marked with ticks), bottom row the eight accents (#B58900 yellow, #CB4B16 orange, #DC322F red, #D33682 magenta, #6C71C4 violet, #268BD2 blue, #2AA198 cyan, #859900 green) arranged around a small color-wheel inset showing their fixed angular relationships; thin connector lines showing which four monotones serve dark mode vs light mode, demonstrating the symmetric swap. Neutral light-gray background, minimal sans-serif labels.
verify_note: Year and designer correct. Minor: sources date the open-source release to April 2011, so the why-text's 'Published March 2011' is slightly early.

name: Google Material Design
lesson: Affordance can be restored to flat design with one honest physical cue: consistent light casting consistent shadows.
why: Announced at I/O in June 2014, 'quantum paper' made every surface a sheet at a quantized elevation with codified shadows from 1dp to 24dp, laid out on an 8dp baseline grid, with the 56dp circular floating action button as the canonical raised control. One year after iOS 7 (2013) flattened affordances away, Material gave buttons back their pressability using physics instead of gloss.
fal_prompt: Recreate a 2014 Material Design specimen in HTML/CSS on a light #FAFAFA ground: a white card (2dp shadow: soft 1-3px ambient plus tighter key shadow) containing a 24px Roboto-style headline, 14px body text, and two flat uppercase text buttons in indigo #3F51B5; beside it a raised rectangular button at 4dp, and a 56px circular floating action button in pink #FF4081 at 6dp with a centered plus glyph drawn in CSS; align everything to a visible faint 8px baseline grid overlay toggleable via a checkbox. The shadows must visibly differ by elevation level so the z-axis hierarchy reads at a glance.
verify_note: Announced June 25, 2014 at Google I/O; 'Quantum Paper' codename confirmed.

name: Mac OS X Aqua interface
designer: Apple Human Interface team under Steve Jobs
lesson: A control should announce what it does before you touch it — affordance through material cues like gloss, depth, and color-position coding.
why: Unveiled at Macworld San Francisco in January 2000, Aqua's gel buttons — specular top highlight, saturated body, soft inner shadow — were so tactile Jobs said 'we made the buttons on the screen look so good you'll want to lick them.' The red/yellow/green traffic-light window controls encode close/minimize/zoom by both color and fixed position, and the default button pulses to declare the primary action.
fal_prompt: Recreate an Aqua-era dialog in HTML/CSS: a window with a brushed pinstripe titlebar (subtle alternating 1px light-gray horizontal stripes), three glossy traffic-light orbs top-left (red #FF5F57, yellow #FEBC2E, green #28C840, each with a white specular ellipse highlight at upper third and a soft inner shadow); body area in pale pinstripe; two capsule buttons bottom-right — one neutral gray gel, one bright Aqua-blue gel default button built from layered CSS gradients (saturated blue body, white 40%-opacity highlight ellipse on the top half, darker blue rim) with a slow 1.2s opacity pulse animation on the default. The gel depth must come entirely from gradients and shadows, no images.
verify_note: Unveiled January 5, 2000 at Macworld San Francisco; Jobs's 'lick' quote documented.

name: The Yellow Fade Technique (Basecamp)
designer: 37signals (Jason Fried's team; popularized via Signal vs. Noise)
lesson: Motion's first job is communication: one well-timed fade that says 'this is what changed' beats a screenful of animation.
why: After a save, the edited row flashes a pale yellow (#FFFF99-family) highlight that fades to transparent over roughly one to three seconds — a single animated property, run once, never looping. Published on Signal vs. Noise in 2004 and shipped in Basecamp, it became the canonical Ajax-era feedback pattern precisely because it is the minimum possible motion that still carries meaning.
fal_prompt: Recreate the Yellow Fade Technique live in HTML/CSS: a plain 2004-style task list on white — 13px Verdana rows with thin gray separators, an 'Edit' link per row; clicking a row's save (simulate with a button) swaps its text and triggers a CSS animation: background-color starts at #FFFF99 and eases to transparent over 2 seconds (single run, ease-out). Include three states side by side for teaching: the row at 0s (full yellow), ~1s (half-faded), and 2s (transparent), plus the live animated version. No other motion anywhere on the page.
verify_note: Signal vs. Noise post published February 19, 2004; built for Basecamp's to-do editing as described.

name: Linear
designer: Karri Saarinen, Tuomas Artman, Jori Lallo (Linear)
lesson: Response speed is the feel: instant local-first interactions and short restrained ease-outs read as quality, not animation.
why: Built from 2019 and out of private beta in June 2020, Linear renders every action from a local sync engine so interactions land in tens of milliseconds instead of a server round-trip, with the Cmd+K command menu making every command keyboard-reachable; transitions are short (~100-200ms) ease-out fades and slides, never decorative. Its dark, motion-restrained look became so influential that 'Linear style' is now a named genre of product design.

Everything low-saturation except one indigo accent.

name: CSS Zen Garden
lesson: Identity lives in the constraint system, not the content: change only the stylesheet and you change everything the design is.
why: Launched in May 2003, it serves one fixed, untouchable HTML file that 200+ contributed CSS stylesheets restyle into radically different complete designs — proof that structure and skin are separable and that a coherent set of styling constraints IS the design. It is the founding demonstration of the idea behind every modern design system, including hand-coded multi-theme systems like Shake's five.

Clean white background, restrained labels.

name: Clear to-do list (heat-map gesture UI)
designer: Realmac Software + Impending (Phill Ryu) + Milen Dzhumerov
lesson: Hierarchy can ride on a single channel: map importance to one gradient and position, and the eye reads priority instantly without any chrome.
why: Clear has zero buttons, toolbars, or nav bars — the entire screen is full-bleed list rows tinted on a heat-map gradient from hot red at the top to pale yellow at the bottom, so vertical position literally equals urgency. Squint and the hierarchy survives: the hottest item is always the brightest, topmost block; all interaction (swipe to complete, pull to create, pinch to navigate) lives in gestures, not visible controls.

Each row is a flat rectangle ~62px tall with bold white left-aligned sans-serif text; row backgrounds step through a smooth heat gradient from saturated red (#D93A30) at the top through orange (#E8853A) to warm yellow (#E9B33A) at the bottom. One row mid-list shown mid-swipe, offset ~80px right revealing a green completion layer beneath. 1px darker separators only from the gradient stepping. Optionally animate a pull-down gap at the top showing a new-item row being created.
verify_note: Verified: launched Feb 2012 as collaboration of Realmac Software, Impending (Phill Ryu, David Lanham), and Milen Dzhumerov. Gesture-only heat-map UI confirmed by 2012 coverage.

name: Apple Watch Activity Rings
designer: Apple human interface team (Alan Dye, Kevin Lynch)
lesson: One glance, one focal point: a whole day of data compressed into a single image the eye resolves in under a second.
why: Three concentric round-capped arcs — red Move outermost, lime-green Exercise, cyan Stand innermost — sit on pure #000000 black so the OLED screen dissolves into the bezel and only the rings exist. Progress is read by arc closure alone: no numerals are needed to know you are 80% done, and a closed ring overlapping its own start reads as 'complete' from across the room. The result of a year of design iteration at Apple.

Three concentric ring tracks centered, each track a dim 20%-opacity version of its color; on top, three progress arcs with perfectly round line caps: outer ring saturated red-pink (#FA114F) at ~85% closure, middle ring bright lime green (#92E82A) at ~60%, inner ring cyan (#00D3F2) at ~100% so its round cap overlaps its own start point with a subtle drop shadow showing the overlap. Equal gaps between rings, stroke width about 11% of the ring diameter. No text, no numbers anywhere.
verify_note: Verified: Apple Watch shipped April 2015; Alan Dye (human interface) and Kevin Lynch (technology VP) publicly discussed designing the Watch/Activity features in 2015 Wired interview.

name: Windows Phone 7 'Metro' panorama UI
designer: Microsoft Windows Phone design studio (Albert Shum)
lesson: Type IS the interface: when the typography carries hierarchy and navigation, chrome becomes unnecessary.
why: Launched October 21, 2010, Metro replaced icons and bevels with Segoe WP Light set enormous — lowercase section headers around 65-72pt deliberately clipped off the right screen edge so the cropped letterforms themselves signal 'pan sideways for more.' Its stated principle was 'content before chrome': flat single-color tiles, transit-signage-inspired type, and no gradients, shadows, or glass anywhere — three years before iOS went flat.

Below it a 2-column grid of flat solid tiles in a single accent color (Metro cyan #1BA1E2), square corners, no shadows, no gradients, white glyph-free squares with one-word lowercase labels beneath. A sliver of the next panorama panel peeks in from the right edge to invite horizontal panning.
verify_note: Verified: WP7 launched Oct 21, 2010; Metro design led by Albert Shum's Windows Phone studio, transit-signage inspiration and 'content before chrome' confirmed.

name: iA Writer for iPad (Focus Mode)
lesson: Typographic restraint as a feature: one typeface, one size, zero options forces every design decision into the type itself.
why: Released September 22, 2010, iA Writer offered exactly one font (Nitti Light, a monospace by Bold Monday), one size, and no formatting controls at all — the column was tuned to roughly 9-10 words per line for optimal reading rhythm. Focus Mode dims every sentence except the one being written to a faint grey ghost, proving hierarchy can be made with opacity alone, no second typeface or color required.

A single centered text column of monospaced light-weight type (~19px, generous 1.7 line-height, about 60 characters per line). Focus Mode active: the current sentence in near-black (#1A1A1A), every other line faded to ~25% grey. A tall slim blue (#2F7CF6) caret blinks at the end of the dark sentence via CSS animation. Nothing else on screen.
verify_note: Verified: released Sept 22, 2010 for iPad by Information Architects (Oliver Reichenstein); Nitti monospace by Bold Monday and Focus Mode dimming confirmed.

name: Things 3 (Today list)
lesson: Whitespace is the grouping mechanism: generous, consistent space can replace every divider, border, and box.
why: The May 2017 redesign (Apple Design Award winner that June) draws no separator lines between tasks at all — rows are grouped purely by spacing rhythm, and each row is reduced to a small rounded-square checkbox plus one line of text, with all metadata hidden until tap. Margins are wide and section headings are isolated by white space several times taller than a text line, demonstrating that space, not lines, makes structure.

Two groups separated by a tall band of pure white space and a small bold project heading with a tiny progress-pie glyph. One checked row shows a filled blue checkbox and lighter struck text. Spacing rhythm consistent throughout; total restraint.
verify_note: Verified: Things 3 released May 2017 by Cultured Code; won an Apple Design Award at WWDC 2017.

name: iPhone OS 1 Springboard home screen
designer: Apple (Scott Forstall, Imran Chaudhri, Freddy Anzures)
lesson: A strict grid plus one repeated module turns sixteen different things into one calm composition.
why: The June 2007 home screen locked every app into a fixed 4-column grid of 57x57 px icons, each masked to the identical rounded rectangle with the same top-edge gloss highlight, on black — sixteen wildly different functions reading as one family because the container, not the content, is constant. A reflective dock shelf anchors exactly four icons at the bottom, separating 'always' from 'sometimes' with position alone.

The screen shows a tidy four-column grid of small glossy colorful rounded-square icons over a black background — icons rendered as soft abstract candy-colored shapes with glassy top highlights, slightly out of focus so no text or logos are legible — and a faint reflective shelf at the bottom holding four more icons. Warm late-2000s tungsten indoor lighting, shallow depth of field, 50mm lens, dark neutral grey background, no text anywhere in the image.
verify_note: Verified: original iPhone June 2007; SpringBoard icon grid co-created by Imran Chaudhri with Freddy Anzures under Scott Forstall's software org; 57x57 icon size documented.

name: iOS 7 system redesign
lesson: Neutral foundation plus one accent: strip surfaces to white and let a single tint color mark everything tappable.
why: Unveiled June 2013, iOS 7 deleted leather, linen, and gloss overnight: surfaces became flat white, separators became 1-pixel hairlines, and each app was assigned one 'tint color' (Mail's #007AFF blue, Notes' yellow) applied to every interactive element — buttons lost their borders and became colored text. Depth moved from fake drop shadows to honest translucent blur layers, a material the screen could actually be.

Below, list rows of ultra-light large type with 1px #C8C7CC hairline separators inset from the left, small grey chevrons on the right, and one blue dot unread indicator. Everything flat: zero gradients, zero shadows except the blur layer. The only color on screen is the single blue tint.
verify_note: Verified: unveiled June 10, 2013 at WWDC; flat redesign led by Jony Ive with Alan Dye on the human interface team.

name: Instagram monochrome app redesign
lesson: When content is the color, the chrome must go grayscale — reserve saturation for the thing that matters.
why: In May 2016 Spalter's team stripped Instagram's blue chrome to pure black-and-white: thin outline glyphs on white bars, with Spalter stating the color 'should come directly from the community's photos and videos.' The square photo became the only saturated region on screen — a one-rule color system (chrome 0% saturation, content 100%) that also improved accessibility and still governs the app a decade later.

Below it a row of thin black outline glyphs: heart, speech bubble, paper plane, bookmark — all pure black line icons, no fills, no color. Bottom tab bar: five thin black outline glyphs on white. The gradient square must be the only saturated color on the page.

name: Slide to Unlock
designer: Apple (Imran Chaudhri, Bas Ording, Freddy Anzures, Greg Christie et al.)
lesson: An affordance announces itself: a recessed groove, a knob, and an arrow tell the finger exactly what to do before any words are read.
why: The 2007 lock screen control (patent filed December 2005) is a complete affordance lesson in one widget: a track visibly recessed with an inner shadow says 'something travels here,' a glossy raised slider says 'grab me,' and the embossed right-pointing arrow says 'that way.' A light sheen sweeps left-to-right across the label about once per second, animating the exact direction of the required gesture.

At the left end sits a raised glossy slider button: silver vertical gradient, rounded corners, with a chevron-style right-pointing arrow etched on it. Centered in the track, grey label text with a CSS animation sweeping a bright diagonal shimmer band through the letters left to right on a ~2.5s loop. Make the slider draggable; releasing early springs it back to the left with an ease-out bounce.
verify_note: Verified: shipped on 2007 iPhone; patent filed Dec 2005 with inventors Chaudhri, Ording, Anzures, Christie plus Forstall, van Os, Lemay — 'et al.' covers the rest.

name: iPhone Calculator app (Braun homage)
designer: Apple, after Dieter Rams & Dietrich Lubs' Braun ET44/ET66
lesson: Great proportion systems are inheritable: a 1977 keypad's button geometry and color-coding transplanted intact into software thirty years later.
why: The 2007 iOS Calculator copied the keypad of the Braun ET44 (1977) and ET66 (1987) by Rams and Lubs almost cell for cell: a strict 4-column grid of convex rounded keys, dark muted number keys, and operators isolated in a distinct color column so function is read by hue and position before any symbol. It is the clearest proof on the original home screen that proportion and color-coding — not decoration — are what made the hardware classic work.
fal_prompt: Recreate the 2007 iPhone Calculator in HTML/CSS: top quarter is a dark display panel with a huge thin right-aligned numeral; below, a strict 4-column keypad grid. Number keys: dark charcoal rounded-rectangle buttons with a subtle convex vertical gradient and soft top highlight, white centered labels. Function row along the top of the keypad in lighter grey; the entire right-hand operator column in saturated orange (#FF9500-style) with white symbols. Equal gutters everywhere, every key the same height, zero key larger spanning two columns. Add a faint pressed state that flattens the gradient to show the convexity is doing the affordance work.
verify_note: Verified: 2007 iOS Calculator's resemblance to Braun ET44 (1977) / ET66 (1987) by Lubs and Rams is widely documented (Fast Company, Cult of Mac).

name: Rubber-band overscroll (inertial scrolling)
lesson: Physics is feedback: an edge communicated by stretch-and-spring feels truthful in a way no dialog or hard stop can.
why: Ording's 2005 demo — shipped on the iPhone in 2007 and shown by Jobs at the January unveiling — lets a list be dragged past its end, stretch with diminishing resistance, then snap back with an ease-out spring, proving the device hadn't frozen and giving content apparent mass.
